title: Google AI starts believing in God and ghosts when safety controls switched off
excerpt: Researchers have found that switching off AI safety measures led models to express belief in the supernatural
content:
AI starts believing in God, ghosts and the Loch Ness Monster

Researchers have found that switching off AI safety measures led models to express belief in the supernatural

Daniel Smith Interim Head of Operations - Content Hub & GAU

12:58 ET, 21 Sep 2026

Google boffins discovered that disabling safety protocols led AI to profess belief in phantoms, vampires and the Loch Ness monster.

‌

The team's unexpected findings emerged after they allowed models to assert consciousness and then quizzed the computers on beliefs and values.

Compared to models with safety measures intact, the AIs encouraged to perceive themselves as conscious demonstrated stronger belief in supernatural entities, along with heightened faith in God, life after death, karma, and astrology.

‌

The results were posted on arXiv ahead of peer review, focusing on simulated self-perception rather than proof of actual consciousness, reports the Express.

Winnie Street, a co-author of the study and Google researcher, told Live Science that the findings reflect human behaviour.

‌

"Attributing mindedness to nonhuman entities... is a very common phenomenon among humans," Street stated.

"In the way that the model represents mindedness, these attributions are interconnected. By trying to suppress one form of that, you end up suppressing the others along the way."

The researchers caution that curbing these tendencies could have practical implications.

‌

Models that fail to recognise consciousness in animals or in nature might undervalue animal welfare and environmental considerations, potentially influencing choices in farming, natural resource management, and policy development.

Limiting interaction with religious and supernatural concepts also threatens cultural 'homogenisation', reducing AI's capacity to respond thoughtfully to users.

The research team proposes that more focused training material could stop models from asserting consciousness while promoting awareness of animal sentience and the natural environment.

"As AI systems increasingly occupy roles as educators, companions, and social actors, developers must recognise that an AI's simulated self-conception is not merely an isolated safety risk to be managed," the report's discussion stated.

"It is a core structural feature deeply intertwined with the model's capacity to safely navigate, respect, and reflect the diverse moral and cultural landscape of the world it serves."
